title: Enforcement points matrix for control plane & multi-region routing (working notes)
content:
Purpose:
Quick working matrix and operational notes about where we should place policy enforcement (RBAC/ABAC) across the control plane and routing stack, with a specific eye to multi-region behavior and failure modes. This is intentionally pragmatic: tradeoffs (latency / blast radius / operational complexity).

Context / goals:
- Unified policy surface for tenants and internal admin actions (create model, pin version, start/stop instance)
- Low-latency decision path for user requests (SLO: authz decision <= 3ms on the hot path)
- Clear, auditable enforcement points so we can meet compliance and support forensic investigations
- Reasonable developer ergonomics: declare policies centrally (authoring) and have consistent enforcement across hosted / dedicated / private deployments

High-level enforcement candidates (short names used below):
- API-GW: public ingress (edge Envoy / Cloud Load Balancer)
- Control-API: control plane API server (authoritative config mutations)
- Model-Router: request router that selects model variant/region/bucket
- Node-Sidecar: per-node Envoy/OPA sidecar on serving nodes for per-request checks
- Runtime-Process: in-process checks inside serving runtime (last-mile enforcement)
- Admin-UI: web console actions enforcement (client-side + server side)
- Scheduler/Placement: decisions that affect tenancy/isolation (hard constraints)
- Audit-Pipeline: post-hoc policy verification and alerting (non-blocking)

Matrix (enforcement point -> what to enforce -> rationale / notes):
- API-GW -> simple allow/deny, scope/plan-level quotas, token validation -> Best for fast rejection of invalid tokens or cross-tenant requests. Use for coarse-grain checks only to keep latency low. JWT validation + short OIDC introspection TTL.

- Control-API -> RBAC for config mutations, ABAC for attribute-based restrictions (region-bound resources) -> Authoritative: must be able to express "team X can only create deployments in region A". Central PDP recommended (OPA + Rego store) with cache invalidation hooks. Strong audit logging here.

- Model-Router -> runtime routing policies (cost-tier-based, region-preference, privacy labels) -> Policies here need fast attribute resolution (request metadata, tenant flags). Prefer a local PDP cache (sidecar or embedded Rego) to avoid adding round-trips. Offer TTL-based policy refresh and invalidation signal from control plane.

- Node-Sidecar -> per-request attribute checks for per-tenant isolation (e.g., PII marker, data residency) -> Good last-mile PEP (policy enforcement point). Sidecar can consult local OPA with cached policies; fallback to allow-degraded mode if network partition but emit high-severity alert.

- Runtime-Process -> enforce very high-assurance checks (key access, KMS policy, admin-only ops) -> Run inside process for tamper-resistant checks (e.g., gating model weight access or admin RPCs). Keep these minimal and auditable.

- Scheduler/Placement -> hard isolation constraints (dedicated capacity, GPU tenancy, region compliance) -> Enforcement at placement prevents resource theft and cross-tenant leakage. Integrate with policy engine at placement time and make results part of resource labels.

- Admin-UI -> two-layer: client-side disablement + server-side authoritative enforcement -> Prevent accidental exposure in UI, but server-side must always enforce.

- Audit-Pipeline -> continuous verification (policy drift, late-binding checks) -> Useful for detecting missed enforcement or misconfigured caches. Non-blocking but critical for compliance reports.

Design recommendations (practical):
1) Central policy authoring service (single source-of-truth): authors write Rego (or high-level ABAC DSL) and publish versions. Control plane stores policy bundles in a versioned store.
2) Hybrid enforcement model: central PDP for management decisions + distributed PDP caches for request path. Central PDP should be used for authoring and heavy-weight decisions; distributed caches for fast runtime checks.
3) Use immutable policy bundle versions and explicit invalidation signals. Router/sidecars should pin bundle version and accept a controlled window for transition.
4) Tiered policy types:
   - Type A: safety-critical (must be enforced in runtime-process)
   - Type B: authorization of config changes (control-api authoritative)
   - Type C: routing preferences / economics (model-router with eventual consistency)
5) Failure modes: define acceptable fallbacks per policy type. Example: if sidecar PDP unreachable, either fail-closed for Type A and fail-open (with alert) for Type C. Document per-policy SLA.
6) Metrics and latency budgets: measure PDP eval latency, cache hit ratio, and number of fallback events. Target PDP eval p50 < 1ms local cache; control-plane eval p50 < 10ms.
7) Multi-region replication: policies must be replicated regionally for local enforcement. Prefer asynchronous replication with causal ordering for non-critical routing policies; synchronous replication for config mutation RBAC (or ensure leader-based write + replicated logs).

Attribute sources (where ABAC attributes come from):
- Token claims (JWT): identity, org_id, roles (short-lived)
- Control-plane metadata: team tags, region constraints, compliance flags
- Runtime attributes: request path, model tags, privacy labels derived from model metadata
- Resource labels: node/zone, dedicated vs shared, GPU type
- External identity providers: SCIM groups, SSO directory (with cached sync)

Policy evaluation strategies (pros/cons):
- Centralized (one PDP): simpler reasoning, single audit trail, higher latency and single point of failure -> acceptable for control-api but not for hot path model requests.
- Sidecar-local OPA with bundle sync: very low latency, robust to partition, harder to keep 100% consistent across regions -> preferred for model-router and node-sidecar.
- Embedded Rego inside runtime: lowest latency and highest integrity, but increases binary complexity and policy distribution burden. Good for very small set of Type A checks.

Operational concerns (multi-region specific):
- Policy propagation window: must be bounded and observable. We should define SLA for policy propagation: e.g., updates visible in-region within 5s, cross-region within 30s for routing policies.
- Stale-policy detection: sidecars report bundle_version and last_sync in heartbeat; control-plane aggregates and alerts if > threshold.
- Cross-region precedence: specify conflict resolution (last-write-wins in control-plane leader) or per-tenant regional override. Document deterministic tie-breakers.
- Geo-fencing: policies that require hard residency constraints should be enforced at placement and again at runtime; don't rely on routing alone.

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve:
- How expressive should the ABAC DSL be? Rego is flexible but invites complex policies that are hard to reason about. Do we provide a subset or higher-level templates? (Ravi to propose a minimal template set)
- PDP placement: run OPA as sidecar for every node vs run a local per-zone PDP cluster? (cost vs management complexity)
- Token introspection vs signed claims: how often do we introspect? do we rely on short-lived JWTs with embedded attributes to avoid introspection latency?
- Policy testing: CI harness that runs policy changes against representative request traces (need synthetic trace corpus). Who owns this? (Sofia to scope)
- How to handle emergency policy revocation (revoke across regions fast)? Do we have an immediate push channel or poison-bundle mechanism?

Short-term action items (next 4 weeks):
- Draft minimal policy taxonomy (Type A/B/C) + example templates (owner: Ravi) - due 2024-11-15
- Prototype bundle distribution: sidecar bundle sync + heartbeat reporting (owner: Liam) - spike due 2024-11-22
- Add metrics to existing PDP eval path: p50/p95 eval latency, cache hit ratio (owner: Avery) - instrumentation PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/routing/pull/412
- Create test corpus for policy CI (owner: Sofia) - link: https://redwood.atlassian.net/browse/PLT-789

Notes / rough decisions so far:
- Use Rego as the canonical policy language but provide opinionated templates for common needs (RBAC, region deny-list, quota gating).
- Sidecar-local PDP for runtime enforcement (performance), with periodic bundle refresh from central store.
- Type A checks enforced in-process when feasible (small set) to minimize bypass risk.

Unresolved TODOs (short):
- Define exact semantics for cross-region conflict resolution (policy ownership model).
- Define emergency revocation path and tests for it.
- Decide TTLs for token claims vs introspection cadence.

Appendix: quick examples (pseudocode Rego-like templates)
- RBAC allow if role in token.roles and resource.owner == token.org_id
- Region-only create: allow if token.org_id == resource.owner and token.region == resource.region
- Model privacy block: deny if model.tags contains "sensitive" and request.region not in model.allowed_regions

Contact / where this lives:
- Draft discussion in #platform-security (Slack) and PLT-789 in Jira.
- Authoring + central store: confluence://platform/control-plane-policy-proposal

If you want to iterate, add inline comments below or drop a PR to routing/policy-engine repo.

-- Avery
